newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ gov't paints rosy pre-election economic picture.
newsitem.headline: NZ gov't paints rosy pre-election economic picture.

text.p: New Zealand's Treasury forecast steady growth and ballooning surpluses in its pre-election snapshot of the economy on Thursday but analysts sounded a mild note of caution.

Treasury said growth would dip only slightly from earlier forecasts to 2.5 percent in the year to March and bounce back to 3.7 percent the following year, underpinned by a new round of tax cuts planned for July 1997.

"The growth forecasts, I think, particularly for 96/97, are a bit on the optimistic side relative to where we see things going, and I think most others as well," said ANZ chief economist Paul Stewart.
The government reported a record operating surplus of $3.314 billion (US$2.3 billion) in the year to June 1996 and forecast this to rise to nearly double by the year 2000.
"That opens up very exciting options for the government at that time. It can choose from the mix of more social spending, more debt reduction and further tax cuts," Finance Minister Bill Birch said.
The conservative National Party has presided over a vigorous recovery since the early 1990s and portrays itself to voters as guarantor of further economic success.

The opposition Labour Party, which wants more emphasis on social, health and education spending, said the strong figures showed it could implement its promises and still run surpluses and repay debt, though at a slower rate.

But New Zealand First, the party of economic sovereignty which is running neck-and-neck with Labour at second in the opinion polls, said the government was presiding over a "lolly scramble" with recent promises of higher spending.

Labour, New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance are jointly drawing more than 50 percent support in opinion polls. Though divided amongst themselves, they may be able to oust National in the October 12 election, New Zealand's first under proportional representation.
Economists agreed that the government had scored important political points with the portrayal of a healthy economy.

"In terms of the big picture, you've got big solid surpluses and debt being repaid at a rate of knots. It keeps your options open for spending or tax cuts in the future," said SBC Warburg economist Robin Clements.
Treasury said that signs of abating inflationary pressures would allow monetary conditions to ease gradually from the December 1996 quarter, which economists said mirrored the market's expectations.
Net public debt as a percentage of GDP would fall to 27.6 percent by June 1997 from the current 32.5 percent and Treasury forecast it would shrink to 13.3 percent by 2000.
Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank said the Treasury had traditionally been more bullish in its economic outlook than other forecasters, but its track record has been good.
"The Treasury has always had a stronger view of the economy than virtually any other forecaster, and on average over the last five years they've been proved right," he said.
Financial markets showed little reaction to the figures, with attention more keenly focused on the central Reserve Bank's latest economic projections on Friday morning.
